extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society and learned practitioners (mariners/navigators, artists, natural historians, miners, botanists)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical methods for determining longitude at sea by astronomical observations (rising/setting times, equal altitudes of sun or stars) and practical watch-handling/recording rules to apply those methods aboard ship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitude by observing the rising and setting of the sun and watches
rubrics_metrics.description: At the rising and setting of the sun, when half above the horizon, mark the time of the day shown by the watches. Reckon by the watches the time elapsed between the two observations, add half of it to the time of the rising, and you will have the time by the watches when the sun was at south; to which is to be added the equation of the present day by the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sum (time-of-meridian plus equation) equals 12 hours, the ship was at the meridian where the watches were set; if more than 12, the ship was west by as many 15-degree increments as the excess, and if less, east by the deficit. Refractions of morning and evening differ little at sea so cause little error; this method requires neither the height of the pole nor declination nor astronomical instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative: observe setting then next morning rising to find midnight longitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of observing rising then setting, observe the setting first and then next morning the rising, marking at both times the time shown by the watches; then find, by the same manner, the longitude of the place where the ship was at midnight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same arithmetic (half the elapsed interval added to the earlier observation, plus equation) applied to setting+next rising to determine the time of meridian passage at midnight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative: two equal altitudes of the sun before and after noon
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe before and after noon two equal altitudes of the sun, noting the time shown by the watches, and reckon in the same manner as with rising and setting to find when the sun was at south.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altitudes are best taken when the sun is about east or west. In sailing north or south, do not take observations at rising and setting but when the sun is due east and west.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using two equal altitudes of a known star to find longitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Take two equal altitudes of some known star that rises high above the horizon; from these you find the time by the watches when the star was in the south, and using the star's right ascension (and the sun's), calculate the time to compare with the watches to determine longitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method parallels the sun-altitude method; it requires knowledge of the star's right ascension and the sun's and is useful when the star rises high above the horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when watches differ after having run correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: If watches that have gone exactly for a while afterwards differ from one another, it will be best to reckon by that which goes fastest, unless you perceive an apparent cause why it goes too fast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: pendulum watches are more easily slowed than made faster; the wire of the pendulum may stretch (making it slow) but cannot grow shorter, and a small weight may slip downwards but not up. Thus the fastest-going watch is the likeliest to reflect true elapsed time absent a known cause of fast running.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record known longitudes of land to correct sea charts and adjust watches
rubrics_metrics.description: When you get sight of any known country, island, or coast, be sure to note their longitude as exactly as you can by the rules prescribed; thereby you may correct sea maps and know how far you have sailed east or west.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If by accident the watches stop, you may at a place whose longitude is certainly known set them going again and adjust them there by the sun and so reckon longitudes from that meridian.

rubrics_metrics.name: If all watches stop set them going quickly to track east/west progress
rubrics_metrics.description: If all the watches should stop at sea, you must, as speedily as possible, set them going again, that you may know how much you advance from that place towards the east or west.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing east/west advance is important because currents can carry the ship so that even when sailing before the wind one may be driven astern; use log-line or other ordinary reckoning or past 24-hour observations to estimate drift in the interim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine examples with precepts in art instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: For teaching the arts it is necessary to join examples to precepts; examine works of the most excellent painters and make observations informing others wherein the perfection of a picture consists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular conference/examination of masterworks discloses secrets of the art not capturable by written rules and gives occasion to discuss important otherwise untreated questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression in painting depends on surrounding bodies and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression particularly depends on the bodies which environ the figures; surrounding elements set out the motion and action in the figure and can make a painted figure seem to have life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Raphael's combat of St. Michael, the press of air by a descending body causes other elements to be driven up, conveying motion and life to the principal figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of colours and light to emphasize or sink parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ordering of colours and light to make certain parts stand out and others recede: wrap presenting legs in very white linen and clothe supporting figures in vivid colours to bring forward or sink parts by placing shadows deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temper neighbouring colours so the eye may pass gradually from one to another; prevent adjacent vivid colours from clashing by turning up sleeves or other devices to create intermediary tonal transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrast (figures and tones) to enhance carnation and focal points
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasting adjacent figures and tones (e.g., a child in brown, a man in black, and a negro beside a bright carnation) can produce admirable contrast that makes carnation or focal features appear more vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic placement of dark and light subjects near a focal face or figure increases perceived splendour and luminosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by varied postures suited to persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Different characters should be given different postures appropriate to their nature; postures express character—youths in active poses, industrious gatherers bent, a girl unwilling to stoop holding out her coat to express a soft temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning varied postures across figures in a scene clarifies character differences and narrative intent; observe age/genius conventions (e.g., old men peeping, doubting miracles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sap issues in proportion to twig/root size
rubrics_metrics.description: In birch trees, the sap issues out of the least twigs of branches and fibres of roots in proportion to their size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation-based rule: expect relative bleed rates to scale with cross-sectional size of the wounded element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches bent downward issue more sap than erect ones
rubrics_metrics.description: From branches that bend downward there issues a great deal more sap than from others of the same size in a more erect posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posture influences bleeding intensity; control for posture when comparing sap flow among branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted/trimmed branches and roots bleeding behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Branches and young trees cut quite off when full of sap and held perpendicularly will bleed; if their tops are cut off and they are inverted they will bleed also at the small ends. Roots cut asunder will bleed both ways but faster from the part remaining on the tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature can alter relative bleeding rates (e.g., cold days may reverse faster-bleeding side). Bear in mind seasonality: wounds made before sap rises will bleed when sap rises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sap ascends in bark, between coats, and through the wood — detection method
rubrics_metrics.description: Sap ascends not only between bark and tree and in pricked circles between coats of wood, but also through the very body of the wood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of detection: cut a branch trunk, immediately hold white paper on the cut top, mark wet spots with pins; distribution of pins (some in circles, some in wood between) demonstrates sap pathways. Cutting opposite slopes to a narrow edge composed only of wood also shows sap reaching the edge, wetting paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method to test direction of sap flow using bored hole and sawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Bore a hole in a large birch that yields drops periodically; saw into the trunk deeper than the hole first below, then above, and observe changes in bleeding from the hole and sawed furrows to infer sap movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the reported experiment sawing below diminished bleeding about half; sawing above ceased the hole's bleeding and produced bleeding at both sawed furrows, showing movement both ways or pressure relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation by age and temperature in bleeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Some trees of the same kind and age bleed faster and sooner than others; but old trees always sooner and faster than young. Very cold weather can abate or cease bleeding in some species while provoking abundant bleeding in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track species-specific responses: birches ceased bleeding when very cold then resumed as it warmed; sycamores and walnuts behaved differently under same thermal changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willows planted with wrong ends may root and grow backwards
rubrics_metrics.description: Set several willows with the wrong ends downward; the cut briars that had taken root at the small ends will produce shoots and backward growth from the part left to the roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed on 29 May: sets shot branches near two feet long and produced great leaves ready to flower — practical planting implication for propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence and remedies for 'damps' in deep mines
rubrics_metrics.description: Damps occur in most deep mines, in both horizontal passages (cuniculi) and vertical pits (putei), in clayey and rocky ground; some are weak causing faintness, others suffocate quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies: ventilation by perflation (letting air in and out) using long tubes or continual bellows; place tubes over doors and ways; in severe cases force a broad flat board down to stop the pit except for the tube and force air out through the tube until fresh air enters via other passages. Long tubes let miners dig far without breath impediment; ventilation placement and repeated purging may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other mine hazards beyond damps: fire and impregnated water
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides poisonous exhalations, miners sometimes perish by wood set on fire (smothering) or by water impregnated with mineral spirits; great quantities of timber in mines increase fire risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take precautions against ignition of large timber supports; provide multiple ventilation paths and tubes and avoid careless use of lights; historical example: wood fire in Chremnitz gold mine smothered many men.
